did.unittitle: J.A. Bailey photograph album of Mombasa and Zanzibar
did.abstract: One album, containing 205 photographs, chiefly of Mombasa and Zanzibar, collected by the business agent for the Christian Missionary Society in Mombasa, J.A. Bailey (1864-1942). Included are images of the missionary settlement of formerly enslaved people, Frere Town; as well as images of Zanzibar, including its ruler at the time, Sultan Said Hamid al-Thuwani al-Busaidi (1857-1896). Also included are photographs of Bailey's family, of locations in England, and souvenir photographs of travels in Egypt, Jerusalem and other locations.

accessrestrict.head: Conditions governing access
accessrestrict.p: The J.A. Bailey photograph album of Mombasa and Zanzibar (MC.119) is open and available for use in the Archives and Special Collections department of the New York University Abu Dhabi Library.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The contents of the J.A. Bailey album are described in the original order in which items were arranged by the creator of the album, presumably Bailey himself. Rather than being arranged in strict chronological order, the photographs are presented in a seemingly random order, where photographs of his time in Mombasa are interspersed with images taken or collected during his periods of home leave in England, or with materials from travels in the wider region. Some images have captions that include dates, while most do not, but of the images that are dated, they are typically not arranged in any sequential or chronological order.

bioghist.head: Biographical note
bioghist.p: J.A. (John Anthony) Bailey (1864-1942) was born in Hulme, Lancashire, England on 14 January 1864, to Joseph and Margaret Bailey. Not much is known about his early life, but the 1881 Census shows him as living with Thomas and Caroline Tinley of Kidderminster, Worcestershire, and as being listed as their son. He was 18 at that time, and his profession was listed as "cashier." He completed his education at Greenheys School in Manchester, and sources show him as having arrived in East Africa in 1885, and being appointed as an accountant with the British East Africa mission of the Church Missionary Society (CMS) in Mombasa in 1889.

Mary Wase (née Harvey) Bailey (1860-1947) was born in Crimplesham, Norfolk, England on 24 March 1860 to Burton and Sarah Bailey. She had one older sister, who appears to have died in childhood, and a younger brother, and the earliest census records (1861) show that in addition to her parents and sisters, five servants lived in their home, suggesting that they were a family of some means. Little else is known of Mary Wase Harvey during this period, other than that by the 1881 Census, only her mother and brother are listed as living with her in Crimplesham, and one servant.

In 1885, she was accepted into the Church Missionary Society, having trained and worked as a deaconess at The Willows, the training center in Stoke Newington, London, which was run at the time by Mildmay Institutions, and which was subsequently taken over by the CMS. In 1888, she was sent to the East Equatorial African Mission in Frere Town, British East Africa (now part of modern day Mombasa, Kenya). It is likely there that she met J.A. Bailey, as the two were married there on 11 May 1892.

During the following decade, the Baileys had three sons: Anthony Drummond (1893-1916), who later served in the British Army during World War I as a second-lieutenant and was killed following the Battle of the Somme in December 1916; Cuthbert Lionel Wase (1899-1954), who became an Anglican priest serving in parishes in England and Scotland; and Basil Noel Victor (1900-1951), who became a physician, later serving at a government hospital in British Guiana. The Baileys lived in and around the coastal city of Mombasa for two decades, with likely most of that time spent in Frere Town, a settlement where the CMS worked with formerly enslaved Africans. Records show that they left on furlough at least three times, from April - November 1893, March - October 1897, and November 1900 to June 1901.

While J.A. Bailey continued to work as an accountant with the British East Africa Mission of the CMS, it appears from records that he performed similar functions with other organizations in the region, including the Uganda and Usagara Mission of the CMS, for which he acted as a coastal agent, and the British Foreign and Bible Society, for which he is listed as an agent in Mombasa in 1909. It is not known when the Baileys left East Africa, and later immigration records show them returning to London from Shanghai, where they had been listed as residents, in 1919. Upon their return, they settled in Suffolk, eventually living in Greenhaven, Rumburgh. Records show that both of their surviving sons were married in 1929, with Cuthbert marrying Nellie Stephen in Toronto, and Basil marrying Ena Elizabeth Meade in Epsom, Surrey.
J.A. Bailey died in Norwich, on 1 July 1942, and Mary Wase Bailey died on 15 October 1947 at her home in Greenhaven, Rumburgh.

processinfo.head: Processing information
processinfo.p: The description of the contents of the album combines captions used by the album's creator, which are usually represented in quotation marks, with those provided by the processing archivist, which are either without quotation marks or in brackets. Since the album is not paginated, the processing archivist added page numbers in brackets, in order to identify the location of each photo or groups of photos in the album. Processed by Brad Bauer, July 2026.

scopecontent.head: Content Description
scopecontent.p: The J.A. Bailey collection consists one photograph album, containing 205 images, chiefly from Mombasa and Zanzibar during the 1890s, collected by the business agent for the Christian Missionary Society (CMS) in Mombasa, J.A. Bailey (1864-1942). Included are images of the missionary settlement of formerly enslaved people, Frere Town; as well as images of Zanzibar, including its ruler at the time, Sultan Said Hamid al-Thuwani al-Busaidi (1857-1896). Also included are photographs of Bailey's family, of locations in England, and souvenir photographs of travels in Egypt and Jerusalem.

The core of this collection consists of images, presumably created by Bailey, showing daily life and activities in Frere Town, a settlement founded by the CMS in 1874 as a refuge for Africans who had been enslaved elsewhere on the continent (typically in southern and eastern Africa), and who had been then been freed as a result of British-led anti-slavery campaigns, typically the breaking up of Arab-led slave trading networks in the western Indian Ocean region. The settlement was named after Sir Bartle Frere (1815-1884), the former British governor of India, who had been sent by the British government in 1873 to negotiate with the Sultan of Zanzibar for an end to the slave trade in the region. The following year, 600 acres were set aside on the outskirts of Mombasa, and formerly enslaved people who had been taken to Bombay following their liberation from slave-trading ships were relocated to Frere Town, and given the opportunity to learn trades, attend school, and some of them received theological training and formed the basis of the "native clergy" that were ordained and appointed to serve in the newly formed church there. Each of these activities are reflected in the images held in this album, which depicts the residents of Frere Town, local scenery, the schools, student dormitories, the hospital, and the "New Church," as well as some of the African clergy and their families, as well as British missioners.

Bailey also included images of the areas surrounding Frere Town, including the old town (and the Portuguese fort) in Mombasa, and surrounding communities such as Kilindini harbor, Mzizima, and the inland settlement of Rabai, where the CMS also had a mission station. Bailey traveled to Zanzibar at least once, yet although a couple of images appear to be his, most of the images were commercially produced ones, such as those documenting the aftermath of the British attack on Zanzibar City in 1896, as well as images of the ruling Sultan Hamid bin Thuwaini (ruled: 1893-1896).

Interspersed with the images from East Africa are photographs from England, as well as of Bailey's immediate family and friends and relatives. These were likely taken during the furloughs granted to Bailey and his family during the 1890s, with scenes ranging from Kidderminster to the West Country and London, including images of The Willows, the training facility for CMS missioners in Stoke Newington, London. Toward the end of the album, there are many commercially produced images from Egypt and Palestine, as well as a few other locations (Istanbul, Athens), which although undated, were likely acquired during travels in these regions during Bailey's furlough of 1900-1901, and include images produced by the Zangaki Brothers in Egypt, depicting pyramids, churches, and archaeological sites, and those of the American Community in Jerusalem, with images that Christian pilgrims often sought out in Jerusalem and the surrounding region.

userestrict.head: Conditions governing use
userestrict.p: The copyright status of the contents of this collection are unknown, and some content within the collection may be protected by copyright. Any uses of such material beyond what is commonly accepted as "fair use" require the express written permission of the copyright holder.
